hero.title: Current Electricity — From Drift Velocity to Kirchhoff's Laws
hero.hook: Current Electricity is the foundation of all electrical engineering. Ohm's Law, Kirchhoff's Laws, Wheatstone Bridge, metre bridge — these concepts connect to every electrical device ever made. It's also one of the highest-scoring chapters in Class 12 Physics boards, often worth 7–8 marks in numericals alone.

hook_section.scenario: In a copper wire, there are about 10²³ free electrons per cm³ — but they move in random directions. No net current. Apply a battery: they still move randomly, but now they also drift slightly toward the positive terminal. This tiny drift velocity (~10⁻⁴ m/s, much slower than you'd think) is what creates current. 1 Ampere = 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons passing per second.
hook_section.bridge: Current Electricity (Chapter 3) builds on Class 10 electricity. New concepts: drift velocity, Ohm's Law derivation, resistivity and its factors, combination of cells, Kirchhoff's Laws (KCL + KVL), and bridge circuits (Wheatstone, metre bridge). These are tested every year.
hook_section.punchline: I = nAevd (drift velocity formula). Ohm's Law from microscopic picture. Kirchhoff's Laws for complex circuits. These three unlock the whole chapter.

concept_section.analogy: Drift velocity is like a river current in a busy sea. Water molecules (electrons) move in all random directions (thermal motion), but the river has a net flow in one direction (drift). The current is not because electrons move fast — it's because there are so many of them and they all drift together, however slowly. I = nAevd shows how even a tiny drift velocity produces large currents.
concept_section.principle: Drift velocity: vd = eEτ/m = J/ne (J = current density, n = electron density, τ = relaxation time). Ohm's Law: V = IR, where R = ρl/A (ρ = resistivity). Kirchhoff's Laws: KCL (sum of currents at junction = 0, charge conservation); KVL (sum of EMF = sum of IR drops in a loop, energy conservation).

reveals.question: 🔵 Drift velocity and current?
reveals.answer: I = nAevd. n = number of free electrons per unit volume (electron density), A = cross-sectional area, e = electron charge, vd = drift velocity. Drift velocity is very small (~10⁻⁴ m/s) but current is large because n is huge (~10²⁸ /m³ in copper).

reveals.question: 🌡️ Resistivity and temperature?
reveals.answer: R = ρl/A. Resistivity ρ depends on material and temperature. For metals: ρ increases with temperature (more vibrations, more collisions, less drift). For semiconductors: ρ decreases with temperature (more charge carriers freed). Temperature coefficient α: ρT = ρ₀(1+αT).

reveals.question: 🔄 Kirchhoff's Laws — application?
reveals.answer: KCL (Junction rule): ΣI = 0 at any junction. Currents in = currents out. KVL (Loop rule): ΣV = 0 around any closed loop. ΣE = ΣIR. Strategy: assign current directions, write KCL at junctions, write KVL for loops, solve simultaneous equations.

reveals.question: ⚖️ Wheatstone Bridge?
reveals.answer: Four resistors P, Q, R, S in a diamond arrangement with galvanometer between midpoints. Balance condition: P/Q = R/S (no current through galvanometer). Metre bridge is a practical Wheatstone bridge: X/R = l/(100−l) where l is balance length on 100cm wire.

points: Drift velocity: I = nAevd; responsible for electric current in conductors
Ohm's Law: V = IR; R = ρl/A; ρ for metals increases with temperature
KCL: sum of currents at junction = 0 (charge conservation)
KVL: sum of EMF = sum of IR drops in any closed loop (energy conservation)
Wheatstone balance: P/Q = R/S; metre bridge: X/R = l/(100−l)

exam_questions.question: Using Kirchhoff's Laws, find the current through each branch of the circuit with two cells and three resistors (numerical given in exam).
Define drift velocity. Derive the relation I = nAevd.
State Kirchhoff's current law. On what conservation principle is it based?

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's Current Law is based on:
quiz.exp: KCL states the sum of currents at a junction is zero — meaning charge doesn't accumulate at a junction. This is conservation of electric charge.

quiz.q: In a metre bridge experiment, balance length is 60cm. If R = 10Ω, unknown X =
Resistivity of a metal increases with temperature because:
opts: More lattice vibrations increase collision frequency
quiz.exp: As temperature rises, metal ions vibrate more. Free electrons collide more frequently with these vibrating ions, reducing drift velocity and increasing resistance/resistivity.

quiz.q: Drift velocity of electrons in a conductor is of the order:
quiz.exp: Drift velocity is surprisingly slow — about 10⁻⁴ m/s (0.1 mm/s). Yet current effects propagate near the speed of light because the electric field propagates through the conductor almost instantly.

flipcards.back: vd = eEτ/m or I = nAevd (n=electron density, A=area, e=charge, vd=drift velocity)
R = ρl/A; ρ = resistivity (Ω·m), l = length, A = cross-sectional area
The algebraic sum of all EMFs and potential drops in a closed loop = 0 (ΣE = ΣIR)
P/Q = R/S — when galvanometer reads zero (no current through it)

flipcards.back: X/R = l/(100−l) where l is balance length on 100cm wire
Positive — resistance increases with temperature. Semiconductors: negative (resistance decreases with temp)
